what_its_for: Piperacillin is an antibiotic used to treat serious bacterial infections in different parts of the body, including the lungs, skin, urinary tract, stomach, bones, and blood. It works by killing the bacteria causing your infection. It is usually given in a hospital setting.
how_to_take: Piperacillin is given as an injection or intravenous (IV) infusion directly into a vein or muscle. A nurse or healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital will give you this medication. You will NOT inject this yourself at home unless specifically trained and instructed by your healthcare team. Make sure to tell your nurse if the injection site becomes red, swollen, or painful.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose based on your type of infection, your weight, kidney function, and overall health. Doses are typically given every 4 to 6 hours. Always follow your doctor's or nurse's exact instructions. Do not skip doses or stop treatment early, even if you feel better, because this can allow the infection to come back or become harder to treat.
missed_dose: Since this medication is usually given by a healthcare professional in a hospital or clinic, a missed dose will be handled by your care team. If you are receiving treatment at home with nursing support, contact your home health nurse or doctor right away if a dose is missed or delayed. Do not try to double up on doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: Piperacillin is stored and prepared by pharmacy or hospital staff. If you have been sent home with prepared doses, keep them refrigerated as instructed (usually between 36°F and 46°F or 2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze unless told to do so. Keep it out of reach of children. Check the expiration date on the label and do not use it if it has expired or if the solution looks cloudy, discolored, or has particles in it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking other antibiotics, blood thinners, or medications without first telling your doctor, as some drugs can interact with piperacillin. Avoid drinking alcohol during your treatment, as it may increase side effects. Let your doctor know about all vitamins, supplements, and over-the-counter medications you take. Do not stop your treatment early without talking to your doctor first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help right away if you experience: a severe allergic reaction (rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, difficulty breathing, or dizziness); severe diarrhea that is watery or bloody (this could be a sign of a serious gut infection called C. diff); seizures; unusual bruising or bleeding; yellowing of the skin or eyes; dark urine; or signs of kidney problems such as decreased urination or swelling in the legs. Also call if your infection does not seem to be getting better after a few days of treatment.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within a few days of starting piperacillin, but it is very important to complete the full course of treatment your doctor prescribed. Even if your symptoms improve quickly, the infection may not be fully gone. Stopping early can lead to the infection coming back and becoming harder to treat.
special_populations: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing this medication. If you have kidney disease, your doctor may need to adjust your dose. If you are allergic to penicillin, cephalosporins, or other antibiotics, tell your doctor immediately before receiving this medication, as you may also be allergic to piperacillin. Older adults and children may need special dose adjustments based on kidney function and body weight.
